titleText.es: Los otros dos siguen perdidos en el plano infinito con densidad uniforme.
titleText.en: The other two are still lost on the infinite plane of uniform density.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive and official xkcd source both identify comic #669. The Spanish title text directly translates the official note about the two missing subjects. The raster restores the DÓNDE accent, corrects ALGUIEN, joins ROZAMIENTO and EMBUSTEROS across printed line breaks, and leaves the fading marks after ME untranscribed because no further lexical word is visible.

applications.explanationEn: Ha is the present helper for a singular event, and pasado is pasar's completed-action form in the question.
Qué carries a written accent because it directly asks what happened.
Dónde carries a written accent because it directly asks for a location.

excludedUnits.rationale: FSSSSSSSSS is a fading or transport sound effect rather than a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: JE. PARECE QUE A LOS PROFESORES DE FÍSICA NO LES GUSTA TRABAJAR EN EL VACÍO Y SIN ROZAMIENTO DESPUÉS DE TODO.

applications.explanationEn: Parece and que form the conventional introduction to an apparent conclusion.

applications.exampleEs: A LOS PROFESORES DE FÍSICA NO LES GUSTA TRABAJAR
applications.explanationEn: A los profesores names the plural group, no makes the preference negative, les points back to that group, and trabajar remains in its unchanged -ar dictionary form.
The three words work together as a final reconsidering expression rather than a literal sequence in time.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Pasado is the completed-action form of pasar. In qué ha pasado, pasar means to happen rather than to move past a place.
Dónde carries a written accent when it directly or indirectly asks about a location. In a direct question, Spanish also uses the opening question mark ¿.
Spanish uses a form of estar, rather than ser, to say where someone or something is. Estoy is the form for the speaker.
At the start of a stand-alone wish, que introduces the hoped-for event and is followed by a special subjunctive verb form.
Spanish writes laughter with repeated j sounds, such as ja, je, ji, jo, or ju. Je can suggest a restrained, knowing, or slightly awkward laugh.

cards.answerEn: Parece que… means “It seems that…” or “It looks as though…”
cards.noteEn: Put a complete statement after que. Use this pattern when the available evidence points toward a conclusion, but you are not presenting that conclusion as completely certain.
cards.questionEn: How do you introduce something that seems likely but is not certain?

example.en: It looks like it is going to rain.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces the person who likes something
cards.noteEn: With gustar, a can introduce or clarify the person experiencing the liking. A quien means “to whom” in the Spanish structure even when natural English simply says “who likes.”

example.es: Es una amiga a quien le gusta bailar.
example.en: She is a friend who likes dancing.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that a named group of people likes or dislikes doing an activity?
cards.answerEn: Name the group after a, use les, then gusta, then the activity verb in its unchanged dictionary form; put no before les to make it negative.
cards.noteEn: Les points back to the named group. Gusta stays singular because an activity is treated as one liked thing, and the activity verb remains in its dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Spanish therefore says a mis amigos les gusta correr, even though the friends are plural.

example.es: A mis vecinos no les gusta madrugar.
example.en: My neighbors do not like getting up early.

cards.questionEn: Why are a vacuum and zero friction central to the joke?
cards.answerEn: Physics problems often remove air resistance and friction to create simple idealized models; the comic turns those assumptions into a place where real professors have been deposited.
cards.noteEn: Ideal conditions make equations easier by eliminating forces that complicate motion. The experiment treats those textbook simplifications as a literal environment and then mocks the professors for disliking the conditions they routinely impose on imagined objects. The official title text adds that two other subjects remain lost on an infinite plane of uniform density.

cards.answerEn: to them; marks the group that likes or dislikes something
cards.noteEn: With gustar, les identifies several people who experience the liking. It does not by itself mean “they.”

example.es: A mis amigos les gusta bailar.

cards.answerEn: they like; is pleasing to them
cards.noteEn: Gusta remains singular when what is liked is one activity in its unchanged dictionary form, even when the people who like it are plural.
In physics, el vacío is a region treated as containing no matter or air.

example.es: La cámara funciona en el vacío.
example.en: The chamber works in a vacuum.

cards.noteEn: Rozamiento is the resistive force between surfaces or through a medium; fricción is a common synonym.

cards.answerEn: after all (as part of después de todo)
cards.noteEn: Después begins the fixed expression después de todo, which adds a conclusion or correction after considering the circumstances.

cards.questionEn: How do you add “after all” when giving a final reason, reminder, or changed conclusion?
cards.noteEn: The three words stay together as a discourse expression. It does not normally refer to one event occurring later than everything else; instead it asks the listener to consider all the circumstances before the conclusion.

example.es: Después de todo, no fue tan difícil.
example.en: After all, it was not so difficult.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; middle of después de todo
cards.noteEn: De links después and todo inside the fixed expression después de todo.

cards.answerEn: all (completing después de todo, after all)
cards.noteEn: Todo completes the fixed expression después de todo.

example.en: After all, it turned out well.

cards.noteEn: Embusteros is masculine or mixed plural. The feminine plural form is embusteras.
